This response argues that its marketing strategies were largely effective in achieving that objective, because its promotion and relationship strategies were well matched to the segment, but that a poorly integrated pricing decision weakened the result and made the gain less likely to last.

Northline's strategies were chosen for the objective rather than inherited from habit. Before 2023 it relied on print advertising, which reached parents more than teenagers. Market research in late 2022 found that its target segment spent far more time on short-form video platforms than with any print medium, so Northline segmented the market by age and lifestyle and repositioned its promotion around the 13 to 17 year old athlete. That gave every later decision a clear test: does it help Northline win and keep teenage customers?

The most effective strategy was the move from print to short-form video. Northline stopped print campaigns that had cost 19 cents per view and produced 140 short videos featuring young local athletes and six influencers. The cost per view fell to 4 cents, so the same budget reached almost five times as many people, and site visits from 13 to 17 year olds rose by a third within six months. This matters for the share objective because a teenager has to know a brand and visit it before they can buy from it. The limitation is that visits are not purchases: the traffic shows that the videos built awareness, not that they converted it into sales.

The evidence for conversion comes from the loyalty app, a relationship marketing strategy launched in April 2023. Members received early access to new releases and a birthday discount, and by the end of the year the app had 85,000 members. Members bought 2.4 times a year, compared with 1.3 times for non-members. For a share objective this is significant, because share held through repeat buying is cheaper to keep than share bought with advertising every year. The app also made the video campaign more effective, since the customers the videos attracted had a reason to keep coming back. Its weakness is that early-access rewards matter most to customers who are already enthusiastic, so it probably deepened loyalty among existing fans more than it won new ones.

The least effective strategy was price. In June 2023 Northline cut prices across its whole range to convert its new traffic into sales. Volume rose, but average sale value fell by 11 per cent, reducing the margin on every sale. More seriously, the cut contradicted the positioning the videos were building. The videos presented Northline as the brand serious young athletes wear, while the discount told the same customers it was a discount label, and when promotion and price send opposite messages, customers tend to believe the cheaper one. A targeted discount, such as members-only prices through the app, could have encouraged trial without undermining the brand.

Place played a smaller supporting role. Northline opened four regional stores and offered free delivery on online orders over $80, which reached teenagers who had seen the videos but lived far from a store. These stores are a small share of total sales, so their contribution to the share objective is modest.

Weighing the strategies against each other shows why their combined effect was smaller than their separate results suggest. The videos created the first visit and the app turned a first purchase into a habit, so each made the other's spending more productive. The price cut worked against both: it reduced the margin that funded further videos and gave app members less reason to wait for early access when everything was already cheaper. A strategy that undermines the others costs twice, once in its own result and again in theirs, which is why Northline finished short of its target despite two strategies that were clearly working.

Taken together, the evidence supports the judgement that Northline's marketing was largely effective. Its share of the target market rose from 8 to 11 per cent, close to the 12 per cent target. The starting point for any evaluation is whether the strategies were chosen for the objective rather than inherited from habit. Before 2023 Northline relied on print advertising in shopping-centre magazines and local newspapers, a mass-market approach that reached parents more than teenagers. Its market research in late 2022, a survey of 1,200 customers and an analysis of its own website traffic, found that its target segment spent far more time on short-form video platforms than with any print medium. Northline therefore segmented the market by age and lifestyle and repositioned its promotion around the 13 to 17 year old athlete. This is the first sign of a strategy selected for the objective rather than simply continued, and it gave every later decision a clear test: does it help Northline win and keep teenage customers?

The most effective strategy was the move from print advertising to short-form video on social media. In February 2023 Northline stopped its print campaigns, which had cost 19 cents per view, and produced 140 short videos over the year, featuring young local athletes and six influencers with followings in the target age group. The cost per view fell to 4 cents, so the same budget reached almost five times as many people. More importantly, it reached the right people: site visits from 13 to 17 year olds rose by a third within six months. This matters for the share objective because a teenager has to know a brand and visit it before they can buy from it, and the videos made Northline visible where its target buyers actually spend their time. The limitation is that visits are not purchases. On its own, the rise in traffic shows that the promotion strategy built awareness and interest; it does not prove that it converted that interest into sales. The evidence for conversion comes from the second strategy.

Northline's loyalty app, launched in April 2023, was a relationship marketing strategy designed to turn first purchases into repeat purchases. Members received early access to new releases and a birthday discount, and by the end of the year the app had 85,000 members. Members bought 2.4 times a year, compared with 1.3 times for non-members. For a market share objective this is significant. Share that is bought through advertising has to be paid for again every year, while share held through repeat buying is cheaper to keep, because retaining an existing customer costs less than acquiring a new one. The app also supported the online objective, because members were sent notifications that linked straight to the online store, and online orders from members grew faster than store sales. The app was therefore effective in its own right, and it made the video campaign more effective, since the customers the videos attracted had a reason to keep coming back. Its weakness is that early-access rewards matter most to customers who are already enthusiastic, so the app probably did more to deepen loyalty among existing fans than to win teenagers who had never shopped with Northline.

The least effective strategy was price. In June 2023 Northline cut prices across its whole range, hoping to convert the new website traffic into sales. Volume did rise, but average sale value fell by 11 per cent, which reduced the margin on every sale. The more serious problem is that the price cut contradicted the positioning that the promotion strategy was building. The videos presented Northline as the brand that serious young athletes wear, an aspirational and premium image, while the across-the-range discount told the same customers that Northline was a discount label. When promotion and price send opposite messages, customers tend to believe the cheaper message, which makes the premium positioning harder to rebuild. A more targeted approach, such as discounting only last season's stock or offering members-only prices through the app, could have encouraged trial without undermining the brand.

Product and place played supporting roles. Northline extended its training range with a line designed with two of its influencers, which gave the videos something new to promote each month and gave app members a reason to use their early access. It also opened four new stores in regional towns and offered free delivery on online orders over $80. The regional stores reached teenagers who had seen the videos but had no nearby store, and the delivery offer supported the online objective. However, the four stores account for only a small share of total sales, so their contribution to the share objective is modest, and new stores take time to become profitable.

Weighing the strategies against each other shows why their combined effect was smaller than their separate results suggest. The video campaign and the app reinforced each other: the videos created the first visit, and the app turned a first purchase into a habit, so each made the other's spending more productive. The price cut, by contrast, worked against both. It reduced the margin that funded further videos, and it gave app members less reason to wait for early access when everything was already cheaper. A business can recover from a strategy that simply fails, but a strategy that undermines its other strategies costs twice, once in its own result and again in theirs. This is why Northline finished one percentage point short of its target despite two strategies that were clearly working, and why the evaluation of its marketing cannot rest on any single strategy's figures.

Taken together, the evidence supports the judgement that Northline's marketing strategies were largely effective in achieving its objectives. Its share of the 13 to 17 year old market rose from 8 to 11 per cent, close to the 12 per cent target, and online sales to the segment grew as the video and app strategies intended. The strategies worked best where they were integrated, as when the videos attracted new customers and the app kept them, and worst where they were not, as when the price cut undermined the image the videos had built. Because share held by a discount is fragile, the main risk is that some of the gain will be lost when prices return to normal. Northline's marketing was therefore effective in reaching its target segment and building repeat purchase, but only partly effective in securing a lasting gain in share, and its overall success depends on whether it can restore its premium positioning in 2024.
